lesson.title: When a force does work

steps.headline: Counting the effort of a push

lead.text: Push a box along a floor with a steady force and keep a tally of the effort as you go. Suppose a push of 10 N moves the box 3 m. Each metre costs the same, because the push is steady, so the total is the cost of one metre times the number of metres. Call the cost of pushing 10 N over one metre 10 units. Then 3 m costs 30 units.

The size of the push matters in the same way. Push twice as hard over the same 3 m, with 20 N, and every metre costs twice as much, so the total is 60 units. Doubling the distance doubles the tally, and doubling the force doubles it too. A tally that behaves like this is a product: the force multiplied by the distance moved. The next screen gives that product a name.
Each metre of a steady push costs the same amount.

reveal.text: Each metre costs 10 units, so eight metres cost eight times that.

lead.text: Physicists call this product work. When a steady force acts in the direction an object moves, the work it does is the force times the distance moved.
The unit is the joule, written J. One joule is the work done by a force of 1 N over 1 m. A 10 N push over 3 m does 30 J, and the units in our tally were joules all along.

The word has a narrow meaning. A force does work only while the object it acts on moves along it. Hold a bag at arm's length and your arm pushes up on it, but the bag does not move, so that force does no work on it. Your muscles still tire, because they are straining, but that cost is inside your body and does not count as work on the bag.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the same 12 N force acts over 3 m and then over 6 m. Doubling the distance doubles the work, from 36 J to 72 J.

lead.text: A constant 15 N force acts in the same direction as a 4 m move of the object it pushes.

reveal.text: You multiplied force by distance, so the work is positive: the force acts along the move.

lead.text: So far the force and the move pointed the same way. Often they do not. A box sliding across a floor is pushed along, but friction pulls on it the other way. Friction acts against the move, and the work it does is negative. Negative work means the force is taking something away from the movement and not adding to it.

The size is still force times distance, and the sign records which way the force points compared with the move. A box slides 4 m while 5 N of friction acts against it. The friction does −5 × 4 = −20 J of work. A force along the move does positive work and a force against it does negative work.

steps.headline: A box slides 3 m while an 8 N friction force acts against it. Find the work done by friction.

workedSteps.text: Friction points against the displacement, so its work is negative.

steps.headline: A 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its work.

workedSteps.text: The force opposes the move, so the work is negative.
Multiply the force by the distance, with the sign.

steps.headline: Forces at right angles to the move

lead.text: A third case sits between the first two. Carry a tray of drinks across a room at a steady pace. Your hands push up on the tray while the tray moves sideways. The upward force is at right angles to the move, and it does no work, because it neither pushes the tray further along nor holds it back.

Only the part of a force that points along the move counts. A force at right angles has no part along the move, so its work is zero. The support force from a floor does no work on a box sliding across it, for the same reason. A 30 N support force acting while a box moves 5 m does 0 J of work.
A vertical support force acts while the box slides horizontally.

reveal.text: The support force has no part along the move, so its work is zero.

lead.text: A real object usually has several forces on it, and each one does its own work. To find the work of one force, use only that force and the move. A cart is pulled 4 m with 30 N while 10 N of friction acts against it. The pull does 30 × 4 = 120 J, and the friction does −10 × 4 = −40 J.

Adding the works with their signs gives the net work: 120 − 40 = 80 J. This agrees with the net force times the distance, since the net force is 30 − 10 = 20 N and 20 × 4 = 80 J. Positive net work means the forces together are helping the move along, and negative net work means they are holding it back.
Several forces may act on a cart. The work of each is found separately, from that force and the move.

reveal.text: This pull does 70 J. A separate opposing 4 N force over the same 7 m would do −28 J.

lesson.orientation: Calculate signed work for forces along, against and perpendicular to displacement.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Push a heavy box across a room and you feel it. A short shove is easy. A long push is tiring, and a harder push tires you faster. Now hold a heavy bag at arm's length for a minute. Your arm shakes and you are worn out, yet the bag has not moved at all.

Tiredness is a poor measure, because it depends on the person and on how long they take. Physics wants a number that depends only on the push and the move, so that anyone can calculate it and two people can compare. The last lesson ended with a box sliding along against friction, with part of the push used up. That is a good place to start counting.

We begin with a tally of the effort in a steady push and turn it into a rule with a unit. Then we see what happens when the force points against the move or across it, and what to do when several forces act at once. The bag at arm's length gets an answer on the way.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the work done by a force along, against or across a movement.

recap.keyIdea: A force does work Fd when it acts along a displacement: positive along, negative against and zero at right angles. Net work is the signed sum.

blocks.text: You saw that a steady 10 N push over 3 m adds up to 30 J. You found that a 15 N force over 4 m does 60 J, that a 6 N force against a 5 m move does −30 J, and that a 10 N pull over 7 m does 70 J.

recap.nextHook: Work is done on an object, so it must change something about the object. Next we find what the net work on a moving object changes.

questions.prompt: A constant 15 N force acts along a 4 m displacement. Find its work in joules.
hints: Force and displacement point the same way.
Multiply their magnitudes.
Calculate 15 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 60 J. A force along the displacement does positive work: force times distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two numbers. Work is force times distance.
That divides force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A constant 6 N force acts opposite to a 5 m displacement. Find its signed work in joules.
hints: An opposing force does negative work.
Multiply force and distance, retaining the negative sign.
Calculate −6 × 5.
questions.onCorrect: −30 J. A force against the displacement does negative work: it takes energy away.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the force opposes the motion. Its work is negative.
That subtracts the numbers. Work is force times distance.

questions.prompt: A constant 20 N upward support force acts during a 3 m horizontal displacement. Find the work done by this support force in joules.
hints: Look for the force component along displacement.
The vertical force has no horizontal component.
A zero component gives zero work.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The force is perpendicular to displacement, so its work is 0 J.

questions.onCorrect: 0 J. A force at right angles to the displacement does no work.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the distance. The force is at right angles to the motion, so none of it acts along it.
That is the distance. Work needs a part of the force along it, and there is none.

questions.prompt: A constant 10 N pull acts along a 7 m displacement. Find the work done by this pull alone in joules.
hints: The question asks about one force, not the net force.
Use W = Fd for this parallel pull.
Calculate 10 × 7.
questions.onCorrect: 70 J. The pull's work depends on that pull alone, not on other forces.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Work is force times distance.
That divides the force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: You hold a box stationary for 5 s. How much work does your support force do on the box during that time?
hints: Mechanical work depends on displacement, not the duration of effort.

acceptedIdeas: Zero work because displacement is zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The box has no displacement, so this support force does zero mechanical work on it.

choices.label: Zero work because displacement is zero

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Work needs displacement: a force that moves nothing does no mechanical work.

misconceptions.feedback: Time passing does not count. Work needs the object to move along the force.
Gravity does not move the box either. With no displacement, no force does any work.

questions.prompt: A pull does +70 J on a cart and friction does −28 J. All other forces do zero work. What is the net work?
hints: Add work contributions with their signs.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Net work is the signed sum: 70 − 28 = 42 J.

questions.onCorrect: +42 J. Net work is the signed sum of each force's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. Friction's work is negative, so it takes away from the pull's.
The pull does more work than friction takes away, so the net is positive.

questions.prompt: Pushing a box 2 m with a steady push costs 20 units of effort. How many units does the same push cost over 8 m?
hints: How much effort is each metre?
The push is the same, so each metre costs the same.
Multiply the cost per metre by 8.
questions.onCorrect: 80 units. Same push, four times the distance, four times the effort. Physics calls this effort work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the extra distance to the cost. The cost grows in step with the distance.

questions.prompt: A constant 9 N force acts along a 6 m displacement. How much work does it do, in joules?
hints: Do the force and the displacement point the same way?
Then the work is positive.
Multiply the force by the distance.
questions.onCorrect: 54 J. Work is force times displacement along the force. The joule is one newton times one metre.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two numbers. Multiply them.
That divides force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: Why is the work done by friction negative?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

choices.label: Friction is smaller than the push.
Friction does not touch the box.

questions.onCorrect: A force against the displacement does negative work, whatever its size.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide the sign. Direction relative to the movement does.
Friction acts at the surface where it touches. The sign comes from its direction.

questions.prompt: A 12 N pull acts along a 5 m displacement while 9 N of friction acts against it. What is the net work, in joules?
hints: Find the work of each force with its sign.
Friction's work is negative.
Add the two signed works.
questions.onCorrect: +15 J. Add each force's signed work. Friction takes away from the pull's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two works as if both were positive. Friction's work is negative.
That is the net force alone. Multiply by the distance to get work.
